result.summary: The poet opens a hymn praising Pallas Athene as guardian of the city and a fierce goddess who loves war alongside Ares. She protects soldiers going out and returning, and the poet closes by greeting her and asking for good fortune and happiness.

scenes.title: Hymn to Athene, guardian of cities
scenes.summary: The singer announces his song to Pallas Athene, describes her love of war and her protection of warriors, and ends with a prayer for good fortune.

characters.name: Pallas Athene
characters.description: Guardian of the city, dread goddess of war who saves the people going out to war and returning

characters.name: Ares
characters.description: God of war, with whom Athene shares a love of battle

analysis.text: The hymn presents Athene as a protective, martial deity of the city, emphasising her role in keeping the community safe in war.
Homeric Hymns were short invocations sung before recitations or at festivals; this brief example follows the typical pattern of opening, praise and farewell prayer.

fun_facts.text: This is one of the shortest Homeric Hymns, only five lines in this numbering, and it is a different poem from the longer hymns to Athena.

language_notes.text: Pallas is a common title of Athene, of uncertain origin; the hymn uses it alongside her name as a formal address.
"Dread" means awe-inspiring and terrible, not merely frightening; it describes the goddess's fearsome power.
"Hail" is the traditional closing greeting of a Homeric Hymn, here followed by a request for blessing.

context_notes.text: Athene, daughter of Jove, was patron goddess of Athens and of cities generally, and a goddess of war, wisdom and crafts.
Ares is the god of war. Athene shares his interest in battle, though she is often shown as the more disciplined, strategic fighter.
Short Homeric Hymns commonly end by saying farewell to the deity and asking a favor, often promising to remember her in another song.

literary_notes.text: Repeated "and" piles up the sack, the shouting and the battle, giving the sense of war's rushing, crowded noise.
Athene is shown as a protector, balancing her fearsome side with care for those who go out and return.
The singer turns from describing the goddess to speak to her directly, shifting from narration to prayer.
